pos: n. (an ancestor of Joseph in Matthew's genealogy; named twice)
etymology: Greek Azor, representing a Hebrew name of the post-exilic period, commonly connected with 'azar, to help; named twice, Matthew 1:13-14.
biblical_def: Azor belongs to the stretch of Matthew's genealogy that no other book of Scripture records. He is named at the end of one verse and the beginning of the next: “And Zorobabel begat Abiud; and Abiud begat Eliakim; and Eliakim begat Azor” (Matthew 1:13), and “And Azor begat Sadoc; and Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud” (Matthew 1:14). These are the generations between the return from Babylon and the birth of Christ, a stretch the Old Testament leaves in silence; the only record of these men is the one the Holy Ghost gave the church through Matthew. The list runs to its end: “And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16). Note the change in that verse: the chain of begat is broken, and Joseph is called the husband of Mary rather than the father of Jesus, because the virgin birth is about to be stated. Matthew then declares the shape he has given the whole: “So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations” (Matthew 1:17). Azor stands in the third fourteen.

corruption_summary: Matthew's genealogy is called inaccurate because it omits generations, where Matthew himself states the fourteens he has arranged and Hebrew usage allows the omission.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest charge against Matthew 1 is that the arithmetic is wrong: the fourteens do not come out evenly, and names known from Chronicles are missing. The objection assumes a convention the evangelist never claimed. Hebrew genealogy regularly skips generations, and begat means descended from as readily as fathered; Matthew says plainly in verse 17 what arrangement he has made, which is the behaviour of a writer ordering his material, not concealing a mistake. He has given a genealogy constructed to a purpose and told the reader the purpose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Matthew 1:16 is built to protect. Every link in the chain is begat until the last, where Joseph is named the husband of Mary and Jesus is said to be born of whom — of her. Christ took David's legal line through Joseph and His flesh from the virgin, and a column of unknown names is the setting for that distinction.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Joseph in Matthew's genealogy; named twice)
etymology: Greek Elioud, representing a Hebrew name compounded with 'el, God, commonly explained as God of majesty or God my praise; named twice, Matthew 1:14-15.
biblical_def: Eliud is named at the junction of two verses, as the son of Achim and the father of Eleazar: “And Azor begat Sadoc; and Sadoc begat Achim; and Achim begat Eliud” (Matthew 1:14), then “And Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob” (Matthew 1:15). He stands four generations from the end of the list, in the obscure centuries between Malachi and the Gospels. The name is built on 'el, God, and so belongs with the great company of Hebrew names that are confessions — Elijah, Elisha, Elkanah, Eliakim — carried by men of whom nothing else is known. The genealogy's destination is given two verses later: “And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16), and its structure is declared immediately: “So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations” (Matthew 1:17). A man named for God, remembered in one line of a list, in the generations when Israel had no prophet and the promise seemed to have gone quiet.

corruption_summary: The silent centuries are described as a gap in which revelation failed, where Scripture shows the line of promise continuing through them generation by generation.
corruption_paragraphs: The period between the last prophet and the Gospels is commonly treated as a blank in which Israel's faith became something else, and the genealogies are passed over as padding. Matthew 1:13-15 is the answer to that. No prophet spoke in those generations and no history of them is preserved in the canon, and yet the line ran on: Azor, Sadoc, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob — each name a household, a marriage, a son born and a promise carried one step further toward Bethlehem.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's silence is not His absence. He was keeping a genealogy when He was not sending prophets, and the only reason we have these men's names at all is that He meant us to know the chain had never broken. A believer in a quiet season may take the comfort of that list.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy; named once)
etymology: Greek Kosam, representing a Hebrew name commonly connected with qesem, divination, or taken as a shortened form of a longer compound; named once, Luke 3:28.
biblical_def: Cosam is named once, in the long ascending chain of Luke's genealogy: “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28). Luke's list differs from Matthew's in form and in direction. Matthew descends from Abraham to Joseph; Luke ascends from Jesus to Adam, and he opens with a careful qualification: “And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli” (Luke 3:23). The parenthesis is the evangelist's own guard: Jesus was supposed to be Joseph's son and was not. The chain passes through David by another son than Solomon: “Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31). And it does not stop at Abraham: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Cosam stands in a list that ends by placing the Second Adam in the line of the first.

corruption_summary: The two genealogies are called contradictory, where they are differently framed, differently routed, and differently purposed, and Luke flags his own qualification.
corruption_paragraphs: That Matthew and Luke give different lines is the standard proof-text for the claim that the Gospels contradict each other. The texts themselves show the difference is by design. Matthew descends and Luke ascends; Matthew goes through Solomon and Luke through Nathan; Matthew begins at Abraham and Luke runs back to Adam; and Luke writes “as was supposed” over the whole of it. The church has long explained the two as the legal line through Joseph and the natural line through Mary, or as two lines meeting at Heli; either way, two differently-purposed registers are not two conflicting claims.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the last clause Luke writes: the son of Adam, which was the son of God. Matthew shows the King of Israel; Luke shows the Son of Man, kin to every nation, the Second Adam standing where the first fell. A name no one knows, in the middle of that list, is part of the argument.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy; named once)
etymology: Greek Addi, representing a Hebrew name commonly explained as my ornament or my witness; named once, Luke 3:28.
biblical_def: Addi occurs once: “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28). Five men are named in that one verse and nothing is told of any of them but their place in the chain. The verses on either side are of the same kind: “Which was the son of Joanna, which was the son of Rhesa, which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri” (Luke 3:27), and “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29). Luke is building toward two destinations at once: back through David, “which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31), and back past Abraham to the beginning, “which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). The genealogy is placed in the Gospel immediately after the baptism, where the voice from heaven said This is my beloved Son, and immediately before the temptation, where the devil said If thou be the Son of God. Addi's name sits inside that frame.

corruption_summary: Luke's genealogy is treated as a decorative insertion, where its position between the baptism and the temptation makes it part of the Gospel's argument about who Jesus is.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments often regard Luke's list as material the evangelist found and inserted without much thought, and devotional readers skip it. Its placement says otherwise. Luke puts it between the voice at the Jordan declaring the Sonship of Christ and the wilderness where that Sonship is assailed, and he ends it not at Abraham, as a Jewish register would, but at Adam and then at God. The list is doing theological work: it answers the question the next chapter raises.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of the incarnation. Luke the physician, writing for a Greek, traced the Lord's line back through men no one remembers to the father of the whole race, so that no reader of any nation could say the Saviour was not his kinsman.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy; named once)
etymology: Greek Elmodam, representing a Hebrew name compounded with 'el, God; sometimes compared with Almodad of Genesis 10:26; named once, Luke 3:28.
biblical_def: Elmodam occurs once: “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28). He is the son of Er and the father of Cosam, and that is the whole of the record. The next verse continues in the same manner: “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29). The list is introduced with the evangelist's own guard against misunderstanding: “And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli” (Luke 3:23) — that is, the supposition was in the minds of the people, and the Gospel has already told its reader of the conception by the Holy Ghost. The chain runs to its end in one of the most remarkable clauses in Scripture: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Adam is called the son of God because he was made directly by God; and the list that contains Elmodam exists to connect that first son to the only-begotten.

corruption_summary: Adam is treated as a symbol rather than a man, where Luke places him in a genealogy of named individuals and calls him the son of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern theology grants Genesis 1 to 3 as myth while keeping the doctrine of sin, and treats Adam as humanity in figure. Luke 3 is hard to square with that. The evangelist writes one unbroken list of individuals, from a man standing by the Jordan at about thirty years of age back through Joseph, David, Abraham, Noah and Seth, to Adam — and calls Adam the son of God in the same breath and the same construction as the rest. Paul reasons the same way, setting one man's disobedience against one Man's obedience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel requires a historical Adam. If sin came by one man, so did righteousness; if the first head is a figure, the Second is a figure too, and there is nothing left to be saved from or saved by. A name like Elmodam, known only from this verse, is a link in the chain that makes the argument possible.

pos: n. (a son of Shuthelah in the tribe of Ephraim; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eran, commonly explained as watchful, from 'ur, to be awake or watchful; named once, Numbers 26:36.
biblical_def: Eran is named once, in the Ephraimite section of the second wilderness census: “And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the family of the Eranites” (Numbers 26:36). The verse before gives the three chief houses of the tribe: “These are the sons of Ephraim after their families: of Shuthelah, the family of the Shuthalhites: of Becher, the family of the Bachrites: of Tahan, the family of the Tahanites” (Numbers 26:35), and Eran is a further branch within the first of them, so that his family is a house inside a house. Chronicles gives the same line a generation at a time: “And the sons of Ephraim; Shuthelah, and Bered his son, and Tahath his son, and Eladah his son, and Tahath his son” (1 Chronicles 7:20). The tribe is then numbered: “These are the families of the sons of Ephraim according to those that were numbered of them, thirty and two thousand and five hundred. These are the sons of Joseph after their families” (Numbers 26:37). Ephraim was the younger of Joseph's sons and was set before the elder by Jacob's crossed hands, and the tribe would give the northern kingdom its name. Eran is one branch of it, named once, with a name that means watchful.

corruption_summary: Ephraim's precedence over Manasseh is explained as a later justification of northern power, where Genesis records it as a deliberate act of God against human precedence.
corruption_paragraphs: The elevation of Ephraim is often read as a tribal claim written back into the patriarchal narrative to legitimate the northern kingdom. Genesis 48 makes that reading difficult. Joseph himself tries to correct his father's hands and is refused; the blessing is given with a stated reason, that the younger shall be greater; and the account preserves Joseph's displeasure, which is not how a tribe flatters itself. The same pattern runs through Scripture — Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah over Reuben, David over his brothers — and it is the pattern of election, not of propaganda.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's choosing is free. Ephraim's houses were numbered at thirty-two thousand five hundred and Eran's was one branch within one of them; and the whole tribe held its place because an old blind man crossed his hands on purpose.

pos: n. (a son of Gad; named twice)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eri, commonly explained as my watcher or watchful, from 'ur, to watch; named twice, Genesis 46:16 and Numbers 26:16.
biblical_def: Eri is named among the sons of Gad who went down into Egypt: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16), and again in the census, where his house is registered: “Of Ozni, the family of the Oznites: of Eri, the family of the Erites” (Numbers 26:16). Comparing the two lists is instructive: Genesis has Ezbon where Numbers has Ozni, and the translators' margin at Genesis notes the alternatives; the Authorized Version prints each book as it stands and leaves the reader able to see both. Gad's total follows: “These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). The tribe had a particular character in Israel. Jacob's blessing played on its name, and Moses' blessing called it a lion; its men came to David at Ziklag as warriors whose faces were like the faces of lions; and it was Gad, with Reuben, that asked for the land east of Jordan and was held to the promise of fighting first. Eri's name, watchful, belongs to that line.

corruption_summary: Differences between the Genesis and Numbers lists are urged as contradiction, where the Authorized Version prints both and the translators noted the variants in the margin.
corruption_paragraphs: Gad's sons are listed twice with two differences in the names, and the pairing is offered as proof that the Pentateuch is stitched from incompatible sources. The simpler account fits the evidence: men in Israel commonly bore two names, and the second list is taken two centuries later, after a generation in Egypt and a generation in the wilderness. The translators saw the difference and printed the alternatives in the margin rather than levelling the text, which is the behaviour of men handling Scripture as Scripture.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care of God for households through long silence. Eri went down into Egypt in a household of seventy souls and came out as a family in a nation of six hundred thousand fighting men. The register in Numbers is the proof that nothing was lost in between.

pos: n. (a son of Ephraim; and a place near the well Beer-lahai-roi)
etymology: Hebrew Bered, hail, or perhaps scattered; borne by a son of Ephraim at 1 Chronicles 7:20, and by a place in the south at Genesis 16:14.
biblical_def: Bered names two different things in Scripture, and the dictionary keeps both in one entry because the word is one. The man is a descendant of Ephraim: “And the sons of Ephraim; Shuthelah, and Bered his son, and Tahath his son, and Eladah his son, and Tahath his son” (1 Chronicles 7:20) — a chain of fathers and sons in the Ephraimite line, set beside the family registers of the census: “These are the sons of Ephraim after their families: of Shuthelah, the family of the Shuthalhites” (Numbers 26:35). The place lies in the southern wilderness, and it is named to fix the site of the well where the angel met Hagar; Genesis says the well was between Kadesh and Bered. What happened there is the reason the verse is remembered: “And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain in the way to Shur” (Genesis 16:7), and she answered with a name for God that no one had used before: “And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?” (Genesis 16:13). A runaway Egyptian slave-girl, pregnant and in the desert, is the first person in Scripture recorded as giving God a name.

corruption_summary: Hagar's story is enlisted either to indict Scripture for cruelty or to excuse Abram and Sarai; the text condemns their expedient and shows God's mercy to the woman they wronged.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 16 is read today chiefly as evidence against the patriarchs, and sometimes defended by believers as though Abram and Sarai had done nothing much amiss. Neither reading is the text's. Scripture records the scheme without a word of approval, shows it producing jealousy, contempt and flight, and then sends the angel of the LORD not to the household but to the slave in the desert, with a promise for her son. God took the part of the one with no standing, and He did it while the promise still ran through Sarah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the name she gave: Thou God seest me. The well was called the well of him that liveth and seeth, and its place was fixed in the record between Kadesh and Bered so that the spot could be found. God is not too great to be found by a wronged woman in a wilderness, and He let her name Him for it.

pos: n. (the southern limit of the campaign of the four kings; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'El Paran, the oak or terebinth of Paran, from 'elah, an oak or strong tree; the translators' margin offers “the plain of Paran”; named once, Genesis 14:6.
biblical_def: El-paran occurs once, marking how far south the four kings drove before they turned back north: “And the Horites in their mount Seir, unto Elparan, which is by the wilderness” (Genesis 14:6). The campaign is described in the verse before: “And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that were with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim” (Genesis 14:5). This is the first war recorded in Scripture, fought by nine kings over the cities of the plain, and it swept up Abram's nephew. Abram's answer is the first act of war by a man of faith: “And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them unto Dan” (Genesis 14:14). Three hundred and eighteen men of one household overtook the coalition that had broken five nations. And on his return Abram met the priest-king of Salem, and the chapter gives the words of the blessing: “And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all” (Genesis 14:20).

corruption_summary: Genesis 14 is dismissed as legend, where it reads as a campaign record and supplies the Melchizedek priesthood the New Testament builds upon.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 14 is routinely treated as a heroic tale attached to Abram, chiefly because no outside record of the four kings survives. The chapter does not read like legend. It names nine kings, their cities, a route of march with the peoples smitten at each stage, a revolt in the thirteenth year and a campaign in the fourteenth, the number of Abram's household troops, and a dispute over spoil settled by oath. More importantly, it supplies Melchizedek, on whom the epistle to the Hebrews rests the whole argument for a priesthood greater than Aaron's.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the first tithe in Scripture was paid by Abram to a priest-king of Salem who blessed him in the name of the most high God — before the law, before Levi was born, and therefore not a Mosaic institution. A place-name at the far end of a war-march is part of the setting for that.

pos: n. (a town of Asher that the tribe did not take; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Achlab, probably fat or fruitful, from a root meaning milk or fatness; named once, Judges 1:31.
biblical_def: Ahlab occurs once, in a list of failures: “Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob” (Judges 1:31). Seven towns are named, and the result is stated in the next verse with the words in the order that matters: “But the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: for they did not drive them out” (Judges 1:32). The tribe became the resident minority in its own inheritance. The LORD's charge against the nation follows in the next chapter: “And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this?” (Judges 2:2), and the sentence is the hinge of the whole book: “Wherefore I also said, I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you” (Judges 2:3). Ahlab's name probably means fruitful, which is likely why it was kept and not cleared: good land is the hardest kind to be obedient about.

corruption_summary: Partial obedience is treated as reasonable moderation, where Judges records it as disobedience and names the price in the same breath.
corruption_paragraphs: Asher's record is easy to defend on sensible grounds: the coastal cities were strong, the Canaanites were established, and a tribe must live somewhere. That is precisely the reasoning Judges exposes. The command had been plain and the reasons given; what Asher did was keep the fruitful towns and the people in them, and the consequence was not conquest delayed but a tribe living on its neighbours' terms. God's answer was to leave the nations in place as thorns and snares, which is a judgment shaped exactly like the sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that half-obedience is a form of unbelief, and it usually attaches to whatever is most profitable. Seven towns are named in one verse, and the first of them was called fruitful. A believer should read that list and ask which of his own seven he has decided not to take.
